Former CFTC enforcement lawyer Jeff Le Riche attributed the staff reductions to the Trump administration’s pro-crypto stance, which led to the dismissal or departure of key enforcement personnel. Under the Biden administration, the CFTC had pursued cases against crypto firms like Gemini, FTX, and Polymarket, but enforcement slowed after Trump’s inauguration. Joe Konizeski, a former CFTC lawyer, claimed acting chair Caroline Pham ordered the closure of all crypto-related cases, forcing many to leave the agency. Pham, now at MoonPay, did not comment on the allegations. The CFTC also dismissed non-crypto cases, such as a fraud investigation against WorldWideMarkets Inc. Former staff described the agency as prioritizing crypto enforcement over other areas, leading to a decline in regulatory oversight. The Government Accountability Office (GAO) is investigating the CFTC’s staffing cuts, prompted by Sen. Elizabeth Warren’s calls for accountability. CFTC chair Michael Selig, who previously worked for crypto firms, has promoted a lenient regulatory approach, arguing that the agency should focus on rulemaking rather than enforcement. However, former director Brian Young warned that staffing shortages hinder the CFTC’s ability to manage the growing complexity of crypto and prediction markets. The agency has authorized six new prediction markets in 2025, triple the average annual rate, and plans to create its own rules without congressional input. Despite claims of increased staffing in 2026, former employees report the CFTC remains understaffed, struggling to execute Trump’s 2025 crypto executive order. CFTC Inspector General Christopher Skinner urged the agency to prioritize human capital management, while Selig emphasized the need for regulatory clarity in emerging markets. The agency’s reduced enforcement capacity has raised concerns about fraud, with critics accusing platforms like Polymarket and Kalshi of targeting vulnerable groups through deceptive advertising. The CFTC’s diminished oversight has sparked debates over its ability to protect consumers in rapidly expanding financial sectors.

item.title: What to know about Pope Leo's lung cancer diagnosis
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: Health
Pope Leo has been diagnosed with adenocarcinoma, a type of lung cancer that is most common in nonsmokers. Dr. Otis Brawley, an oncologist at Johns Hopkins University, explained that adenocarcinoma accounts for about 20% of lung cancer cases today, many of which occur in nonsmokers. The pope’s cancer was detected early, with a small lesion that was surgically removed. Brawley noted that if the lymph nodes tested negative, the pope’s prognosis is favorable, with minimal need for further treatment beyond occasional CT scans. The surgery, performed via a minimally invasive procedure, is considered a positive sign, as it indicates the cancer is localized and the pope is in good health. Brawley emphasized that the pope’s age of 71 and active lifestyle, including regular exercise like tennis, contribute to his ability to recover. He also mentioned that the pope’s planned trip to Peru in a few weeks is feasible, as patients with similar procedures typically recover within seven to 10 days. Brawley highlighted the importance of early detection and follow-up on abnormal chest scans, noting that many people ignore such findings. He reiterated that smoking remains the leading cause of lung cancer, though the pope is a nonsmoker. The doctor stressed that the pope’s transparency about his condition and proactive approach to treatment are key factors in his likely positive outcome.

item.title: How one antibiotic morning-after pill came to be widely available in San Francisco
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: Health
A new antibiotic pill called Doxy PEP, short for doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis, has become widely available in San Francisco, offering gay men and trans women protection against bacterial sexually transmitted infections (STIs). The medication, taken one to two days after unprotected sex, has been shown to significantly reduce STI rates. In 2022, San Francisco health officials began recommending Doxy PEP for individuals who had bacterial STIs in the past year, a policy later adopted by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Last year, syphilis rates dropped by 24%, chlamydia by 18%, though gonorrhea saw only a 5% decline. Doctors warn that widespread use of Doxy PEP could contribute to antibiotic resistance, as gonorrhea has already developed resistance to this class of antibiotics. Annie Luetkemeyer of the University of California, San Francisco, emphasized the need for caution, noting that antibiotics are a critical resource and overuse could lead to superbugs. Critics argue condoms should be the primary prevention method, but Luetkemeyer and others counter that condom use remains inconsistent. Vincent Cornelisse, an Australian doctor, questioned the population-level benefits of reducing chlamydia rates, citing its relatively mild consequences compared to syphilis, which can cause blindness, hearing loss, and brain damage. At the Strut clinic in San Francisco, Dr. Hyman Scott and his team offer Doxy PEP to all who could benefit, reflecting a shift from restrictive guidelines seen with HIV prevention medication PrEP, which initially faced access barriers. Scott argued that overprescription of antibiotics for STIs is less concerning than their use in livestock, where large quantities are consumed. He and others stress that the benefits of Doxy PEP in reducing STIs outweigh the risks, while advocating for careful monitoring to mitigate antibiotic resistance. The debate highlights the challenge of balancing public health benefits with the global threat of antimicrobial resistance.

item.title: Don't be scared: Being afraid is outright fun, and maybe useful
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: Health
As Halloween approaches, Americans are expected to spend over $13 billion on seasonal festivities, with haunted attractions accounting for $300 million to $500 million in revenue. Markoff's Haunted Forest in Maryland, one of the country's largest haunted attractions, draws millions annually. The site features over a mile of trails and themed houses, employing hundreds of staff including engineers, makeup artists, and actors. Director Paul Brubacher explains the attraction's design, inspired by music festivals and horror films, with safety measures like emergency radios. Art director Chris Knowles oversees rapid makeup application for scare actors, using airbrushes to create ghouls, vampires, and aliens in under seven minutes. Scare actors like Robert Doyle and Jermaine Hoes describe their roles as entertaining crowds and providing a controlled fear experience, with Doyle noting the dopamine rush from scaring people. The trail itself is designed to immerse visitors in a dark, foggy environment filled with jump scares, snakes, ghosts, and other horror elements. Harvard Medical School's Nouchine Hadjikhani explains that fear triggers the amygdala, causing physical reactions like increased heart rate and sweating, and that even watching others react to fear can activate the same brain responses. Researchers at Aarhus University's Recreational Fear Lab, Matthias Clausen and Marc Andersen, highlight that recreational fear is universal, acting as a 'fear vaccine' to prepare individuals for real-world threats. They also note social bonding during haunts and anecdotal evidence that some use horror media to manage anxiety. The article concludes by emphasizing the blend of fun and utility in seeking fear, with the next installment exploring the financial impact of horror culture.
